title: In how many leaps does the dog catch the rabbit?
description: A dog chases a rabbit that starts one hundred and fifty feet ahead, and each leap of the dog is nine feet against seven feet for the rabbit. The board finds how much the dog gains in one leap, then how many such gains fill the head start, and checks that both have run the same distance.
teaching_notes: One idea: both run the same way, so the dog closes the gap by the difference of the two leaps, and the head start is divided by that gain. Watch for children who add the two leap lengths.

source: A dog is chasing a rabbit that has a head start of 150 feet. It jumps 9 feet every time the rabbit jumps 7 feet. In how many leaps does the dog catch up with the rabbit?
video_script.why: The child has seen a chase as a gap that shrinks by the same amount each leap and now does it with new numbers.
video_script.substitution: The head start is the gap, and each leap shrinks the gap by the dog's leap less the rabbit's leap.
video_script.anchor: a dog and a rabbit on a straight line, the rabbit one hundred and fifty feet ahead
video_script.payoff_line: The dog catches up with the rabbit in seventy five leaps
maths_rules: both run the same way, so in one leap the dog gains 9 - 7 = 2 feet
the gap of 150 feet closes by 2 feet each leap, so leaps = 150 / 2 = 75
check: the dog runs 75 x 9 = 675 feet; the rabbit runs 150 + 75 x 7 = 150 + 525 = 675 feet; they are equal
video_script.design: One straight line, a dog and a rabbit, the head start as a gap that shrinks, as in the cat and mouse example. Assumes taking away and dividing.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, find the gain in one leap, because both run the same way. We take the rabbit's leap away from the dog's leap.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Nine minus seven is two feet.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: number of leaps = head start / gain = 150 / 2

marks.m2: 150 / 2 is written with the gap cut into pieces of 2 ft

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, divide the head start by the gain, because every leap closes two feet of the gap.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>One hundred and fifty divided by two gives the number of leaps.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Check by putting the leaps back in the question. The dog makes one hundred and fifty divided by two leaps of nine feet.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>That is six hundred and seventy five feet. The rabbit runs the head start and the same number of leaps of seven feet.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>That is one hundred and fifty plus five hundred and twenty five feet. Both come to six hundred and seventy five feet.
